Description:
## Overview

The shrine of Akhund Panju Baba stands at Akbarpura, a town in Nowshera District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in the historic Peshawar valley. It honours *Hazrat Syed Abdul Wahab*, known to all as *Akhund Panju Baba*, a Sufi and preacher remembered as one of the great teachers of Islam in the Pashtun country during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar (1556-1605). Tradition holds that many were guided to Islam through him, and that his circle of disciples included some of the most notable saints of the region — among them, it is said, *Bahadur Baba*, the father of the celebrated *Kaka Sahib* of Nowshera, so that Akhund Panju Baba stands near the head of a whole genealogy of Pashtun Sufi teachers. His tomb at Akbarpura, together with the historic mosque associated with him — a Mughal-era foundation reckoned to be some four centuries old — forms a shrine complex attended by thousands of devotees, who gather especially at the annual *urs* to seek his blessing. Set amid the fields and orchards of the Nowshera plain, the shrine is a characteristic example of the Sufi *ziyarat* of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the memory of the early preacher-saints remains woven into the devotional life of the surrounding villages. Its enduring draw testifies to the reverence in which Akhund Panju Baba is held as a founder of the region's Islamic learning and as the spiritual ancestor of a line of saints whose shrines dot the valley.

## A Second Source, a Different Locality

A general compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints separately records an "Akhund Panju Baba" whose shrine it places at Misri Pura, in Peshawar Sadar — a different named locality from Akbarpura, Nowshera District, where this entry's other sourcing places the shrine. That compendium gives a specific origin for the name: it states that opponents mockingly nicknamed him "Panju" ("five") for his insistence on preaching the five pillars of Islam, and that the name stuck. It does not give his birth name, and does not mention Bahadur Baba or Kaka Sahib. Whether this is the same saint remembered with a variant locality tradition, or a distinct Pashtun preacher who happened to share the same by-name — "Akhund [X] Baba" is a common honorific pattern in the region — is not resolvable from these two sources alone, and is reported here rather than silently merged.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
qa_note: A second source (a general tazkira/compendium of Pakistani saints) describes an "Akhund Panju Baba" at Misri Pura, Peshawar Sadar, with a different name-origin story (a mocking nickname for preaching the five pillars of Islam) than this entry's existing sourcing (Akbarpura, Nowshera District; real name Hazrat Syed Abdul Wahab). The two accounts do not name the same locality and do not corroborate each other's specific details. Not resolved as the same or different individuals — reported as an open question. All pre-existing detail in this entry (Bahadur Baba/Kaka Sahib lineage, Mughal-era mosque dating, etc.) predates this session and has no traceable citation of its own; the tazkira citation added here supports only the Misri Pura material in the new second section.

Description:
## Overview

Set beside the Lahore High Court on The Mall, in the shadow of the colonial-era Aiwan-e-Auqaf building that now bears its name, the shrine of Baba Shah Chiragh commemorates Syed Abdul Razzaq, a Sufi of the Qadiri lineage who traced his descent to Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani of Baghdad and whose family originated from Uch in what is now Bahawalpur. Given the honorific "Chiragh," meaning lamp, by his grandfather Hazrat Abdul Qadir Sani, he flourished during the reign of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan and died in 1657 CE. His mausoleum was constructed by imperial order of Aurangzeb, and an adjoining mosque was added later, in 1716, under the patronage of Lahore's Mughal viceroy Zakariya Khan during the reign of Muhammad Shah Rangeela. The mausoleum, built of limestone on a square plan in restrained Mughal style, contains eight graves in total, including those of Shah Chiragh's father and grandfather, making it a multi-generational family shrine rather than a single tomb. Its façades feature cusped-arch niches and panelled cartouches, while the interior retains traces of floral fresco decoration. In the late nineteenth century the surrounding precinct was absorbed into the grand Indo-Saracenic Aiwan-e-Auqaf complex, built by the British administration between 1875 and 1880, which today houses the offices and library of the Auqaf Department — the same body that has administered the shrine since 1973. Though it lacks the international renown of some of Lahore's other Sufi sites, the shrine is formally catalogued as a protected heritage monument by the Punjab Directorate General of Archaeology, and its distinctive Mughal fabric, set incongruously amid the bureaucratic buildings of modern Lahore, makes it a quietly significant survival from the city's seventeenth-century religious landscape.

## Corroborating Sources

An independent English-language academic study of Sufis and pre-colonial Muslim rulers in India, consulted separately from the tazkira below, states in passing that "Aurangzeb gave importance to some other Shari minded Qadri sufi, like Shah Chiragh whose tomb was constructed by Aurangzeb" — corroborating, from an independent scholarly source, this entry's existing claim that Aurangzeb ordered the mausoleum built. (The paper's own full citation details were not recoverable from the OCR text at hand; this should be verified against the original PDF before being treated as a fully resolved citation.) A general compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints separately notes, in its entry on the nearby shrine of Mauj Darya Bukhari, that Mauj Darya Bukhari's own grave lies inside Shah Chiragh's mausoleum complex — a detail about the physical site not previously recorded here.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
- Academic study of Sufis and pre-colonial Muslim rulers of India (full citation to be confirmed from source PDF) — corroborates the Aurangzeb construction date.

## Overview

The shrine of *Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani* is among the most historically important Sufi mausolea of Multan, the "city of saints", and marks the resting place of the man traditionally credited with establishing the *Chishti* order firmly in the city. Born at Multan around 1747 (1160 AH) and dying in 1811, Hafiz Jamal was a disciple of *Khwaja Noor Muhammad Maharvi*, a leading Chishti master of the region, and became a renowned teacher and poet in his own right, composing in Arabic, Persian and Siraiki; his *Siharfi*, an acrostic poem of the Punjabi–Siraiki tradition, is his best-known literary work. His tomb, near the Aam Khas Bagh outside the historic Daulat Gate, is a fine piece of late-Mughal funerary architecture: a square chamber rising to a twelve-sided drum and a hemispherical dome. It is especially valued because it preserves original Mughal-era wall paintings — a rarity, since the murals of most such monuments have been lost to whitewash and renovation. The shrine remains an active centre of devotion, with an annual *urs* commemorating the saint and continuous visitation by those seeking blessing, and it forms part of the dense sacred geography of Multan alongside the great shrines of Bahauddin Zakariya, Shah Rukn-e-Alam and Shah Shams Sabzwari.

## Corroborating Source

A general compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints independently corroborates this entry's central claim, stating plainly that Hafiz Muhammad Jamal Multani was "the first elder to lay the foundation of the Chishtia order" in Multan, and confirms his shrine's location in the city.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 1 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
qa_note: Added an independent citation corroborating the existing claim that this figure first established the Chishti order in Multan. The specific biographical/architectural detail (birth year, Siharfi authorship, wall-painting preservation) predates this session and has no traceable citation of its own; the tazkira supports only the Chishti-founding claim and the shrine's location.

## Overview

The Shrine of Makhdoom Nooh at Hala, a town some fifty-six kilometres north-east of Hyderabad in Sindh, honours one of the most revered saints and scholars of the province. Makhdoom Lutufullah, universally known as Makhdoom Nooh — and often as Makhdoom Sarwar Nooh — is generally dated to the sixteenth century, with tradition placing his birth around 1500-1505 and his death about 1590. A Sufi of the *Suhrawardi* order, honoured also with an Uwaisi spiritual lineage, he is remembered as the founder of the *Sarwari* branch of the order in Sindh, and above all as the first religious scholar of the region to render the Holy Quran into Persian, an achievement that secured his lasting fame. He was buried near his native village close to Halakandi, but the shifting of the Indus twice compelled the relocation of his remains — to Mula Sanwani about 1601, and again, in 1777, to the site of new Hala, where his mausoleum now stands. The shrine is the spiritual heart of Hala, a town long associated with the *Makhdoom* saintly lineage, with Sufi devotional music and with the celebrated blue-and-white *Kashi* pottery of the region. It draws devotees throughout the year and hosts an annual *urs* in the saint's memory.

## Corroborating Source

A general compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints independently confirms his real name as Lutfullah and his title as Makhdoom Nooh, and states that he died at the age of 87 — consistent with this entry's existing dating (birth c.1500-1505, death c.1590, which implies an age of roughly 85-90). It describes his shrine at "Hala Kandi" as a major place of pilgrimage, matching this entry's account of the saint's original burial place near Halakandi.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
qa_note: Added a corroborating citation: an independent tazkira gives the same real name (Lutfullah) and an age at death (87) consistent with this entry's existing birth/death year estimates. The relocation history (to Mula Sanwani 1601, to new Hala 1777) and the Sarwari/Uwaisi lineage detail predate this session and have no traceable citation of their own.

Description:
Tucked away on Edward Road near the old Customs House in Anarkali, the octagonal tomb of Hazrat Meeran Muhammad Shah Bukhari — popularly called "Mauj Darya," or "Wave of the River" — commemorates a saint born in 1533 in Uch Sharif, the son of Safi-ud-Din Bukhari of the Sadaat of that town, a descendant of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari whose genealogy is traced through Syed Jalal-ud-Din Jahaniyan Jahangasht, and an adherent of the Suhrawardi silsila founded by Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan. He became a hafiz-e-Quran in his youth and, according to popular tradition, earned his epithet by miraculously diverting the flood-prone River Ravi away from Lahore; he is remembered, too, as a missionary presence who drew many Hindus and Sikhs to Islam.

Above all he is remembered as a spiritual confidant of the Mughal emperor Akbar. The shrine's tradition relates that the emperor was foretold — through the saint's father — of a windstorm and a lit lamp that would mark the saint's presence at the fort of Chittor; when both signs appeared and the Rajput army surrendered, Akbar became his disciple. Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* preserves an independent, extended telling of this same episode — giving the saint's given name as Miran Muhammad Shah, tracing his descent from Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht and his origins in Uch Sharif, and recounting at length how his prayer and intercession were credited with securing the fort's surrender to Akbar — corroborating, from a separate hagiographical compendium, the tradition already recorded at the shrine. Legend credits him with distributing to the poor a substantial reward Akbar granted him near Batala, and it is said that on the saint's arrival in Lahore the emperor gifted the land on which he settled; his darasgah — the seat of learning where he now lies buried — is said still to hold land documents bearing Akbar's own signature. He died in 1604, the date traditionally taken as the founding of the shrine.

He married twice. His first wife, Syedna Bibi Fatima Sani — remembered as "Bibi Killah," and popularly as Mai Fatima — bore him two sons and rests in a separate shrine facing his own, near the historic Jain Mandir; a second wife bore a third son, of whom tradition tells that he could take the form of a lion. The saint lies in a small graveyard in the company of his family, his spiritual successors and gaddi nasheen, and his cook, Allahu Samad — himself the subject of one of the shrine's most striking tales, in which the saint, to answer sceptics, had his cook sit unharmed in a burning cauldron. Other wonders are recounted of him: a cauldron of rice he blessed during a shortage that fed the people for nearly seven days; brackish irrigation water over which he prayed for local landowners, which turned sweet; and a tree planted in his lifetime — "the blessed tree" — said never to have needed cutting. His langar, devotees say, has continued under his descendants to this day.

Architecturally the tomb is unusual among Lahore's shrines for its octagonal plan, with a low dome, corner towers at each of its eight angles, and a mixture of recessed blind arches and plain panelled facades — a style thought to echo Multani funerary tradition. The shrine gained unwelcome national attention in 2018 when construction of the Orange Line Metro Train's underground Anarkali station demolished its mosque, langar khana and courtyard, with tunnelling reported to pass close to the saint's grave in apparent violation of heritage buffer-zone regulations — an episode that became a flashpoint in Lahore's debates over balancing infrastructure development against protection of religious heritage. Yet devotees hold that for all the government construction pressing around it, nothing has ever tarnished the shrine's beauty.

The shrine remains one of scores of Lahore shrines administered by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department (Mehkama Auqaf), and continues to draw a devoted following. Daily devotion includes the recitation of the Fatiha, the lighting of diyas, the making of vows (mannat) and the presentation of niyaz, and the gatherings of Thursday night (Jummay Raat) remain the busiest of the week. The annual urs is held on the 17th to the 19th of Rabi-ul-Awal, with a Mela Chiraagha (festival of lights), the ceremonial washing (gusal) of the tomb and the changing of its chadar, and langar throughout; some 2,200 to 2,500 visitors are recorded on an ordinary day, rising to between 225,000 and 300,000 across the urs.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.

The shrine of Mian Muhammad Umar Baba lies at Chamkani, a village on the eastern outskirts of Peshawar about seven kilometres from the old city. Mian Umar (traditionally 1671-1776) was a Sufi of the Naqshbandi order — a scholar, poet, social reformer, and historian who is counted, together with Akhund Darweza Baba and the warrior-poet Khushal Khan Khattak, among the great literary and spiritual figures of the Mughal-era Pashtun frontier. Said to have been born near Lahore and to have lived to a great age, he attracted disciples from every rank of society; tradition holds that even Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani), the founder of the Afghan kingdom, visited him and became his devotee. Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* gives a specific account of his death — in the month of Rajab, 1119 AH (approximately 1707-1708 CE) — and records his burial at the village of Chamkani, three miles from Peshawar, consistent with the shrine's location as given above; that date, however, falls roughly seven decades earlier than the 1776 death year given elsewhere in this entry, and the discrepancy is left unresolved here, with both figures reported rather than reconciled. His tomb at Chamkani grew into a shrine and khanqah that remains a place of resort for the surrounding population, drawing its largest crowds at the annual urs, held over the first Wednesday and Thursday of the Islamic month of Rajab, when devotees gather for sermons, collective dhikr, and na'at, and the langar (free kitchen) is served. Like a number of Sufi shrines in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the site was targeted in militant attacks during the years of insurgency in the region, but it endures as an active centre of devotion. It complements the nearby shrine of the saint's contemporary Akhund Darweza Baba, also recorded in this dataset.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 2 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.
qa_note: Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* (vol. 2) records the saint's death in Rajab 1119 AH (approximately 1707-1708 CE), roughly seven decades earlier than the 1776 death year already carried in this entry's Founded/Opened and figure_died fields (traditional lifespan 1671-1776). The two dates conflict and have not been reconciled; both are reported in the Description pending further sourcing.

Description:
In the old riverside locality of Chah Miran, named directly in his honour, stands the tomb of Syed Miran Hussain Zanjani, one of the earliest Muslim missionary figures associated with Lahore. A Hussaini Syed born in 958 CE in Zanjan, in present-day Iran, he travelled to Lahore around 998 CE on the instruction of his spiritual master, Sheikh Abu al-Fazal Khatil, and is remembered to have preached in the city for some thirty-six years, converting large numbers of its inhabitants to Islam well before the Ghaznavid and later Mughal periods reshaped the region's religious landscape. He died in 1042 CE and was buried alongside his brother, Hazrat Musa Hussain Zanjani, whose own shrine lies nearby. The tomb, unusually for a site of such antiquity, rests on a simple raised platform without a dome, standing within what was once a dedicated garden named for the saint — a modest architectural footprint that belies its historical significance as one of Lahore's oldest surviving Islamic devotional sites, predating by centuries the grander Mughal-era shrines for which the city is more widely known. The shrine is formally recognised and maintained by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, and continues to host an annual urs drawing local devotees, alongside its role as the namesake and spiritual anchor of the surrounding Chah Miran neighbourhood on the historic bank of the River Ravi near the old walled city. As one of the earliest attested Sufi graves in the Lahore region, the shrine offers valuable testimony to the gradual, missionary-led spread of Islam in Punjab in the centuries before the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal empire.

A substantial chapter devoted to the saint in Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* traces his family's descent from Imam Musa Kazim through the Zanjan line, and preserves one of Lahore's best-known early Sufi foundation stories: that Ali Hujwiri (Data Ganj Bakhsh) was instructed by his own pir to travel to Lahore and preach, and replied that his senior "pir-brother," Hazrat Shaikh Hussain Zanjani, was already established in the city — only to arrive and find Zanjani's funeral procession already under way. The tazkira's account casts Zanjani as the elder of the two missionary saints credited with Lahore's early Islamization, his death preceding the arrival of the more widely celebrated Data Ganj Bakhsh.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 1 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.

Standing close to the great mausoleum of Data Ganj Bakhsh, in the Walled City's Bhati Gate quarter, the shrine of Peer Makki commemorates Hazrat Syed Azizuddin al-Hassani wal-Hussaini, a scholar-mystic born in Baghdad — the son of Hazrat Peer Syed Abdullah, of a Hasani-Hussaini family of religious scholars that counted Junaid Baghdadi, Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal and Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani among its kin. He is said to have migrated to Mecca in 562 AH, at about the age of thirty, and to have spent twelve years there in ascetic seclusion — hence his popular title "Makki" — before journeying overland to India. Hagiographical accounts hold that he arrived in Lahore in 575 AH (around 1178 CE) by what tradition describes as divine instruction, and remained for some thirty-six years as a teacher of both the exoteric sciences of Islamic law and the esoteric path of the Junaidi Sufi lineage, tracing back to the classical Baghdad master Junayd. He is said to have died in 612 AH (1215 CE). Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* preserves the same broad outline — his given name Azizuddin, his Baghdad origin, and the twelve years spent in seclusion at Mecca that earned him the epithet "Makki" — and adds that on first reaching Lahore he went directly to the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh before settling at the site that became his own; the detail reinforces, without resolving, the chronological tension already noted below between the two saints' conventional dates.

A well-loved anecdote recalls that during Sultan Muhammad Ghori's 1178 siege of Lahore, the besieged governor Khusro Malik sought Peer Makki's prayers, and the saint assured him of six further years of safety. Devotional custom in Lahore holds that pilgrims should pay their respects at Peer Makki's tomb before proceeding to Data Darbar, honouring him as a spiritual forerunner in the same sacred locale — although the popular claim that he personally tutored Data Ganj Bakhsh sits awkwardly with the conventional dating of Ali Hujwiri's death around 1072, a century before Peer Makki's own arrival, and should be understood as devotional tradition rather than strict chronology. A tradition recorded at the shrine itself runs the other way about: when Ali Hujwiri was ordered to migrate to Lahore, he is said to have objected that "Peer Makki is present there, who is enough for Lahore" — only to arrive and find Peer Makki's funeral already underway. Like the tutoring claim, the story fits loosely with the dates, but it carries the shrine's essential teaching: that Lahore has never been without a saint of Allah.

The shrine complex includes an adjoining mosque, the Hazrat Pir Makki Masjid, and is formally administered, like Data Darbar itself, by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department; its tradition is Syed and Ahl-e-Sunnat. Despite its proximity to one of Pakistan's most visited shrines, Peer Makki's own tomb receives markedly fewer pilgrims — some 3,500 to 4,000 on an ordinary day — giving it a more intimate, contemplative atmosphere, though Thursday-night gatherings draw larger crowds, and the narrow street and surrounding Peer Makki Bazaar can make access difficult. The annual urs, held on the 9th to the 11th of Rabi-ul-Awal, fills the quarter with gatherings and dhikr, drums and dhamal, qawwali, the ritual bathing of the shrine and the distribution of offerings, and draws on the order of 400,000 to 500,000 devotees. Many writers — including, it is said at the shrine, authors from the Hindu and Christian communities — have written books about the saint that are still read with interest today.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 1 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.

The Shrine of Pir Baba at Pacha Kalay, in the mountainous Buner District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, honours *Syed Ali Tirmizi* (c. 1502–1583), the Sufi saint universally known as *Pir Baba*, one of the most revered holy figures of the Pashtun lands. Of *Sayyid* descent, he was traditionally said to have been born at Tirmiz in Central Asia (in present-day Uzbekistan) — though some accounts instead give Fergana as his birthplace — and, according to tradition, came to the region in the train of the Mughal advance, settling at Pacha in Buner around the middle of the sixteenth century. From there his spiritual influence spread widely, and he is remembered as a supporter of the early Mughals — the emperor Humayun is said to have granted him lands in Kunar — and as an opponent of the heterodox teacher Bayazid Ansari, the "Pir Roshan." A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, gives his fuller name as Syed Ali Ghawwas Tirmizi and names Akhund Darweza — the Peshawar-based Chishti saint venerated at the Shrine of Akhund Darweza Baba elsewhere in this archive — as his most renowned khalifa (successor). His green-domed mausoleum, which also holds the grave of his son Syed Habibullah, became the nucleus of a devotional complex; an adjoining mosque was raised in the twentieth century, between about 1938 and 1965, under the care of his descendants. The shrine draws great crowds of pilgrims, above all at the annual *urs* commemorating the saint, held from 24 to 26 of the Islamic month of Rajab. Its prominence made it a target during the militancy that afflicted the region: in December 2008 militants attacked the shrine, destroying religious inscriptions and hoardings, and in 2009 it was briefly closed when Taliban fighters seized control of Buner, before being reopened as security was restored. It remains among the most important Sufi shrines of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

## Bibliography

- Alam Faqri, *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, vol. 1 (Lahore) — compendium of the saints of Pakistan.

The Shrine of Shah Abdul Karim stands at Bulri, the town in Tando Muhammad Khan district that bears his name — Bulri Shah Karim — and honours one of the earliest and most influential of the Sindhi Sufi poets. Shah Abdul Karim (1536–1623) was born into a Sayyid family of Matiari but spent most of his life at Bulri, from which he takes his epithet. He is remembered as a mystic of simple, laborious life and as a pioneer of Sindhi devotional verse: he was among the first to weave the folk romances of the land — *Sasui and Punhun*, *Sohni and Mehar*, *Umar and Marui*, *Leela and Chanesar* — into poetry expressing the soul's longing for the Divine, a method later brought to its summit by his celebrated great-great-grandson, Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. A separate source, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, instead calls him Bhittai's great-grandfather (three generations, not four) and adds that he was himself a disciple (*murid*) of Makhdoom Nooh of Hala before settling and preaching at Bulri — the two sources are recorded here as given, without picking one generational count over the other. His sayings and verses were first gathered by a disciple, Mir Daryai Tharawi, in the Persian work *Bayan al-Arifin*, completed in 1630, seven years after the poet's death. Tradition holds that Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai himself stayed two years at Bulri and supervised the building of the shrine complex, laying the foundation of the tomb and its three-domed mosque about 1741 (1154 AH). The dargah remains a vibrant place of devotion, and its annual *urs* draws thousands of pilgrims.

## Bibliography

Both are stated in the Description rather than one being silently preferred.

Description:
The shrine of Baba Shah Jamal, in the locality that now bears his name adjoining Ichhra and opposite Forman Christian College, commemorates Syed Shah Jamal, a Sufi of Hussaini Syed descent who traced his lineage to Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif. He belonged jointly to the Qadiriyya, Suhrawardiyya and Chishtiyya orders — a special disciple, tradition holds, of Sheikh Khokar Baig Suhrawardi — and lived in Lahore during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar, whose syncretic Din-i-Ilahi he is remembered for having resisted, working instead to draw people back towards orthodox Islamic practice. Born, by the shrine's account, in 1587, he is generally held to have died in the later seventeenth century, though sources differ on the precise year: 1649 and 1671 both appear, the shrine's own tradition holding to 1671 and commemorating his death on the 4th of Rabi-ul-Sani. A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently places his shrine on Achhra Road facing west, in Shah Jamal Colony, Lahore — consistent with this entry's own location — and traces his Suhrawardi lineage specifically to Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan.

The site itself, tradition says, was built and named "Damdama" by Shah Jamal in his own lifetime, and it was one of several stations of his austerities: besides his Damdama cell he kept chillas (forty-day retreats) at Sheikhupura, Shah Rehman, Shahdara Lahore and Chanpatpur in India. His death is remembered as inseparable from his devotions: emerging from a chilla, he died as the roof of his cell collapsed, and as people laboured to free him a voice from within is said to have commanded that he not be pulled out, but that his grave be raised over that very spot — which was done.

Legends gather thickly around the Damdama. The best known tells of a princess — Akbar's sister — who, annoyed that the tall tower overlooked her palace, demanded he lower it; the saint performed dhamal on its top floor, and storey after storey sank into the earth until only two remained, whereupon he predicted that her palace would not outlast his — fulfilled, it is said, when Sikh forces later destroyed it. Another tells of a cheating Hindu businessman to whom the saint gave a cantaloupe to feed his wife; twin sons followed, one of whom, named Sheikh Fakhr-ud-Din by Shah Jamal himself, became a devoted lifelong disciple — and the saint is also said to have saved that family by calling them outside moments before their roof collapsed.

Today the shrine is best known not for quiet contemplation but for its exuberant Thursday-night dhamal, when devotees, students, musicians and curious visitors gather from dusk until the early hours as dhol drummers — most famously the late Pappu Sain, whose successors continue the tradition — drive crowds into rhythmic, trance-like dancing, alongside qawwali, langar and the lighting of lamps. This weekly spectacle has made Shah Jamal one of the most written-about expressions of popular Sufi devotional culture in Punjab, and the crowds are considerable: on the order of 10,000 to 15,000 visitors a day, rising to 200,000-250,000 for the annual urs, held on the 3rd to the 5th of Rabi-ul-Sani with the ritual washing (gusal) of the tomb, the offering of the chadar, and drumming and dhamal.

The tomb itself is enclosed within a mosque of relatively modern construction, single-domed with four minarets, reflecting rebuilding rather than preserved Mughal fabric; an adjoining graveyard lies beside it. The shrine — of the Suhrawardi line and the Ahl-e-Sunnat tradition — has been in the care of the government's Auqaf Department since 1960, while the current sajjada nashin, a descendant of the saint, continues to hold Khatam Khawajgan ceremonies. The site illustrates the continuing vitality of shrine-centred devotional practice in Lahore, and its shadows as well: the city's homeless rely on the shrine's langar and offerings, even as questions over noise, crowding and drug use in the vicinity — a real safety concern for pilgrims — have periodically drawn official scrutiny.

Ziarat Kaka Sahib, set among rugged hills roughly twelve kilometres south of Nowshera city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is the shrine of the sixteenth-century Sufi saint *Kaka Sahib*, whose given name was *Syed Kasteer Gul* and who is also remembered by the honorific *Sheikh Rahmkar*. Born, by tradition, on the first of Ramazan in 1575 (sometimes given as 1576), he received his religious education from his Sufi father and from the scholars of his day, and his forefathers are remembered as affiliated with all four of the great Sufi orders — the *Naqshbandi*, *Suhrawardi*, *Chishti*, and *Qadiri* — an inheritance tradition credits him with carrying forward, though he himself is remembered in the *Uwaisi* style of not naming a personal living guide. Tradition names his teachers as Qazi Abul Aala, Abdullah Ansari Sultanpuri, Maulana Abdul Lateef Sultanpuri, and Sheikh Akhuddeen Seljuki; the nearby saint Akhund Panju Baba was a respected contemporary he is said to have met, rather than a personal teacher — Panju Baba's own disciple, by tradition, was Kaka Sahib's father, Bahadur Baba. A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently corroborates his name (there rendered Sheikh Rahm Kar) and adds a specific detail of place: at the time of his birth, his father was living in forest roughly six miles south of the site later known as Ziarat Kaka Sahib. So great was his renown for piety that his resting place became one of the most frequented religious sites of the province, and the town that grew around it took his name. His white mausoleum, raised by his son Sheikh Abdul Haleem around 1661, is a fine example of Mughal-era funerary architecture, richly ornamented within by mosaic work, floral patterns, and painted stucco decoration. The descendants of his teacher and of the saint's own line have long lived in the settlement, tending the shrine and its traditions. Today Ziarat Kaka Sahib remains a much-visited place of pilgrimage, its annual observances drawing devotees from across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa who come to seek blessing at the tomb of a saint whose memory has endured for more than four centuries.

Darbar Abul Muali Qadri is an active Muslim shrine in Lahore, built around the grave of Hazrat Syed Muhammad Khair ul Deen, widely known as Shah Abul Muali Qadri. The complex holds the tomb, a mosque, and a graveyard in which members of the saint's family are buried alongside ordinary and notable dead. It is looked after by the Government Auqaf Department together with the descendants of the shrine's hereditary custodians (*gaddī nashīn* in the surveyor's wording — the *sajjāda nashīn* line). Construction work at the site is ongoing, and between 2,000 and 2,500 people come daily.

## The site and its history
The account given to the surveyor states that in 980 Hijri, when Shah Abul Muali migrated from Depalpur, Okara, to Lahore, he settled at this spot; that during his lifetime the place became a centre for receiving his spiritual blessings; and that he had it constructed and repaired himself. Devotees relate that he was buried here after his passing, and that his tomb was raised at the site of his own seminary, near Mochi Darwaza, where he had earlier built a mosque and taught.

The survey traces custodianship from the saint to his sons and then to the hereditary custodians, names the first custodian as Hazrat Haider Ali Shah — also buried in the shrine — and states that "the kings of every era took care of this place," responsibility passing in the present era to the Auqaf Department. The survey further records that the land for Dyal Singh College in Lahore, close to the shrine, was given by the saint's descendants so that people could acquire education.

## The saint, as the survey relates him
Tradition holds that Shah Abul Muali was born on 10 Zil Hajj 960 Hijri in Kirman, Iran, the son of Syed Rehmatullah Kirmani, of the Kirmani Sadaat. His *kunyat* was Abul Muali, the name by which he is known; the survey also gives his title as Asadullah and describes him as Hassani Hussaini and of the Ahl al-Bayt. His father is described as a scholar and a poet in Urdu and Persian, who migrated from Iran and settled at Depalpur, Okara. Two of his father's brothers are named: Sheikh Dawood Bandgi Kirmani, whose shrine the survey places at Shergarh, and Syed Jalal ud Deen, whose shrine it places in Sindh.

The account states that after his father's death he was taken under the care of his uncle Dawood Bandgi, who was also his father-in-law; that he studied with him until the age of thirty; and that he migrated to Lahore at his uncle's command, establishing there a mosque and seminary near Mochi Darwaza where he led congregational prayers and taught. He is credited with having wells, mosques and *madrasas* built along his route, with writing books in Urdu and Persian, and with composing poetry, though the account is careful to say his focus was preaching. The survey states that he taught and memorised the Quran, possessed both exoteric and esoteric knowledge, and describes him as a dervish and a perfect scholar. Devotees relate that millions pledged allegiance to him, that kings came to him with requests, that he never distinguished between rich and poor, and that he kept many *chillas* (periods of seclusion) and nights of *dhikr* (remembrance of God). The account states that because of him millions of people entered the fold of Islam. He is said to have loved Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani and Mian Mir deeply. It states that he died on 16 Rabi ul Awal 1024 Hijri, during the reign of Shah Jahan, at the age of sixty-five.

Two marriages are recorded: the first to a daughter of Dawood Bandgi Kirmani, who died some time after the marriage, and the second to a daughter of Emperor Shah Jahangir, whose considerable wealth and lands the couple are said to have endowed entirely for charitable purposes. The survey gives him eight sons, buried beside him, one of whom it says was martyred fighting in a war against the Sikhs.

A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently corroborates the saint's identity: it gives his real name as Shah Khairuddin Muhammad, with Abul Ma'ali as his *kunya* — the name by which he became known — matching this entry's own naming. It also describes him as the spiritual guide (*murshid*) of a companion of the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh, a related but distinct claim from the survey's own account above of Dara Shikoh himself receiving the saint's *karāmāt* directly; both are reported rather than merged into one relationship. The tazkira confirms only that his shrine is in Lahore, adding no further detail on the site itself.

## Stories and *karāmāt*
The survey narrates several incidents, which it presents as widely known among devotees.

**The *majzūb* at the roadside.** The account relates that, while still searching for a spiritual master, the saint set out in 980 for the house of a companion, Sheikh Hamid Karishmi, in Delhi. On the way he spoke with a *majzūb* (a spiritually absorbed person) sitting by the road, who told him that the one he was wandering in search of was in his own home, and named his uncle Dawood Bandgi Kirmani. Astonished, he returned to his uncle, who answered with a verse to the effect of: "Wander and see the whole world, blister your feet, if you find anyone like us, then say." His request for allegiance was accepted, and after some days his uncle sent him back to Lahore with the instruction to spend his life in the path of Allah.

**Dreams of Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani.** It is said that whoever pledged allegiance at his hands would see Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani in a dream that very night, and that this was due to his *karāmāt* (miraculous graces).

**The rosary.** The survey cites the Mughal emperor Dara Shikoh — so styled in the account — as writing that he once accompanied Shah Abul Muali to the court of his teacher Sheikh Imam Niyamat Ali, where someone presented the saint with a rosary. Dara Shikoh relates that he silently wished it might be given to him; on their return to the seminary the saint handed him that same rosary, telling him to recite Darood on it daily so that the giver, the recipient and the saint would all share in the reward. He is said to have been amazed that his unspoken thought was known.

**The white turban.** In a second incident attributed to Dara Shikoh, he had never disclosed his love for Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani. One night, the account states, the Sheikh came to him in a dream and gave him a white turban. In the morning, presenting himself before Shah Abul Muali, he was given a white turban by the saint, who said that Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani had asked that it be given to him.

**The rain at the Eidgah.** The survey relates that during a drought at Lahore, when Hakim Afzal Agha was ruling, the Hakim gathered a very large crowd at the Eidgah outside the city for congregational prayer for rain, and came to invite the saint. Shah Abul Muali excused himself, saying he could not walk. The Hakim pressed him, saying that if the saint would not come he too would remain sitting there. At last the saint told him to go, and that it would certainly rain after two days. No rain fell for two days; on the third it rained heavily. When the Hakim returned to ask how he had known, the saint is said to have answered that had it rained on the day of the gathering, the arrogant among the worshippers might have taken it for their own wisdom and it would later have become a cause of sin — so Allah delayed it.

## Devotional life
There is a press of visitors daily. The custodians' descendants live at the shrine, and people travel from far away to receive *dum* (spiritual healing by breath and recitation) from them. The mosque inside the shrine holds the five daily prayers. A gathering is held daily at which *naʿt* (devotional poetry in praise of the Prophet) is recited, and *langar* (free food distribution) is continuous. Every Thursday, drums are beaten, gatherings are held, lamps are lit, and *niyāz* (consecrated offerings of food) is distributed. Devotees also recite Fateha at the graves.

Visitors come to pay their respects and to pray to Allah through the saint's intercession, and the survey reports that they say their prayers are answered there: that whatever the worry or sorrow they find peace only from here, because he had knowledge of the unseen, and that he was a *Wali Allah* (friend of God) from whose door Allah never lets anyone go empty-handed.

## The annual *ʿurs*
The *ʿurs* — the annual commemoration of the saint's death — is held on 15, 16 and 17 Rabi ul Awal. Its programme includes Chadar Poshi (the laying of the shroud), Mela Chiraghan (the festival of lights), a *mehfil* of *naʿt* shareef, dhol and dhamal, *qawwālī*, Ghusal (the ritual washing), and *langar*. The survey gives attendance as 200,000 to 250,000 people.

## Documentation
The surveyor uploaded nine photographs and one audio or video recording; no book or pamphlet was supplied. The survey states that many books have been written on the saint's life and *karāmāt*, that these are easily available, and that his own books are held in the libraries of well-known universities.

The dargah of Luari Sharif, some fifteen kilometres from the town of Badin in the far south of Sindh, is the shrine of Khwaja Muhammad Zaman (1713–1775), one of the most revered Naqshbandi Sufis and Sindhi mystic poets of the eighteenth century. Born into a family of the Siddiqi lineage that claimed descent from the caliph Abu Bakr and had settled in Sindh in earlier centuries, Muhammad Zaman received his first instruction from his father, Shaikh Abdul Latif, a follower of the Naqshbandi order, before studying at Thatta, then the great seat of learning in Sindh. There he came under the influence of the Sufi master Khwaja Abul Masakin, whose disciple he became and from whom, tradition records, he received the honorific Sultan al-Aulia, "master of the saints". Settling at Luari, he made the khanqah he established there — traditionally dated to 1737 — the foremost Naqshbandi centre of eighteenth-century Sindh after Thatta, a place of study from which his khalifas carried the order's teaching across the province. He was also a poet of note; a body of mystical verse in Sindhi is attributed to him, of which some eighty-five poems are said to survive. He died in January 1775 and was buried at Luari, where his tomb and the vaulted chambers of his successors form the shrine complex. An annual urs commemorates him and draws devotees from across the region, though the complex has at times been subject to restricted access, with a police post maintained at its entrance since the 1980s. Luari Sharif is counted among the oldest and most important Sufi sites of southern Sindh.

A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently corroborates the saint's identity and location — recording him as Makhdoom Muhammad Zaman Naqshbandi, known by the title Khwaja Kalan, with his shrine at Luari Sharif, Badin, Sindh — and adds a detail not previously in this entry: that he founded a new town, also named Luari, after the original settlement became uninhabitable. The tazkira gives a year of death, but its digits are illegible in the OCR scan and are not reproduced here.

The town of Pir Jo Goth — "the village of the Pir" — in the Kingri taluka of Khairpur District, Sindh, grew up around the shrine of Pir Syed Muhammad Rashid Shah (1757–1818), known by his honorific Roze Dhani, "master of the shrine," the founder of the Rashidi Sufi order and an ancestor of the line of Pir Pagara. A Qadiri–Naqshbandi saint of great influence, his teaching is said to have spread through Sindh, the Punjab, Balochistan, Rajasthan, and beyond. From his descendants issued the spiritual and temporal leadership of the Hurs, the community of devoted faqirs whose ancestors, under the later Pir Pagaras, waged a celebrated resistance against British rule in Sindh in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; the present (eighth) Pir Pagara draws his authority from this shrine complex. The dargah is distinguished by an austere discipline unusual among Sufi shrines: devotees are required to enter only with the head covered, the Hur faqirs make pilgrimage at fixed times of the year, and the sacred date of 27 Rajab draws great throngs of mureeds — yet, in contrast to the festive urs kept at most Sufi tombs, the Rashidi tradition is said to observe no public urs here. The complex, entered through an imposing Shahi (royal) gate, remains the devotional and political heart of the Hur community and one of the most distinctive shrines of upper Sindh.

A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently places the saint's shrine at Goth Reem Dino, also known as Pir Goth, Sindh, and confirms his descent within the Piran Pagara lineage — consistent with this entry's own account of Pir Jo Goth and the Pir Pagara succession. It also gives a fuller explanation of the epithet "Roze Dhani": tradition holds that as an infant he stopped nursing during the daylight hours of Ramadan, and that the name was later reinforced when a dome (*roza*) was built over his grave.

The shrine of Akhund Darweza Baba lies in the Hazarkhwani area of Peshawar, a short way south of the Ganj gate of the old walled city, where the saint was buried in the historic Hazarkhwani graveyard. *Akhund Darweza* (traditionally 1533-1638) was one of the most influential religious figures of the Pashtun country in the age of the Mughals — a Sufi and a formidable scholar of the outward religious sciences, a poet in both Pashto and Persian, and a disciple of *Sayyid Ali Tirmizi*, the saint known as *Pir Baba* of Buner (himself honoured at a shrine in this collection). He is best remembered for his learned and combative opposition to the *Roshani* movement of Bayazid Ansari (Pir Roshan), against whose teachings he wrote and preached, and for his religious works, among them the *Makhzan al-Islam* and the *Tazkirat al-Abrar wa'l-Ashrar*, which remain landmarks of early Pashto and Indo-Persian religious literature. He died in the reign of Shah Jahan and was laid to rest at Peshawar, where his tomb became, and remains, a place of pilgrimage for those who seek his blessing. The shrine is a characteristic Peshawar *ziyarat*, its custodianship and its customs handed down over the centuries, and it stands as a memorial to a saint who shaped the religious identity of the Pashtuns as both teacher and defender of orthodox belief. Its situation in the crowded graveyards east of the old city ties it to the deep Islamic heritage of Peshawar, the ancient meeting-place of Central Asia and the subcontinent.

A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently corroborates both the shrine's location — giving it as Hazarkhwani, Peshawar, matching this entry — and the saint's discipleship: it names him a *khalifa* (successor) of "Mir Syed Ali," i.e. Syed Ali Ghawwas Tirmizi, the saint venerated as Pir Baba of Buner elsewhere in this archive, confirming the teacher-student relationship already recorded above from the other side at that entry.
